prompt.context: Athelas Insurance company is the leading provider of health insurance in its state. The company has consistently been the lowest cost player in that state. This has enabled them to capture 70% of the state's insured population (4 million insured individuals). Recently, Athelas' senior management has been looking at growth opportunities, and they do not think geographic expansion is a viable option given their expertise. That said, they have been looking to acquire one of the state's largest hospitals, Apollo Inc., which they think is an attractive target. Athelas Insurance has hired you to evaluate the investment and suggest a future course of action.
prompt.question: Evaluate the acquisition of Apollo Inc. by Athelas Insurance. How much should Athelas offer for Apollo? What synergies are needed to meet the return target, and what should Athelas do post-acquisition?

clarifying_info.q: What was Athelas' aim in pursuing the deal?
clarifying_info.a: They don't have a particular aim; they are looking to you to evaluate all synergies.

clarifying_info.q: What does Athelas want to know specifically?
clarifying_info.a: They want to know how much to bid and what to do post-acquisition if they proceed.

clarifying_info.q: What is the background on Apollo Inc.?
clarifying_info.a: Apollo is among the USA's most reputed general hospitals, known for its high quality of care and expertise across all major areas of care. Most patients are extremely loyal and rarely use other hospitals.

clarifying_info.q: Does Athelas have a financial goal for this investment?
clarifying_info.a: They are looking for a 3-year ROI of 30%. Ignore discounting for this calculation.
We will get into that later.

data.excess_capacity: Apollo can absorb up to 200K excess patients without expanding facilities

framework: Valuation of Apollo Inc. on a standalone basis: determine how much to bid (DCF and multiples approach)
ROI target check: derive minimum profit needed over 3 years and gap to standalone value
Synergy identification: brainstorm revenue, cost, and strategic synergies between an insurer and hospital
Synergy sizing: quantify the most feasible synergy (procedure conversion) and test whether it closes the gap
Post-acquisition plan: pricing contract changes, operational steps, risks, and next steps

questions.prompt: How much should Athelas offer for Apollo hospitals Inc.?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use both approaches from Exhibit 1. Approach 1 (DCF): Firm Value = FCF / (Discount Rate - Growth Rate) = $400 Mn / (10% - 0%) = $4 Bn. Note: the casebook uses 12% - 2% = 10% net rate giving $400 Mn / 10% = $4 Bn; the net spread is what matters. Approach 2 (Multiples): Firm Value = EBIT x Average Multiple = $750 Mn x 5.33 = $4 Bn. Both approaches converge at $4 Bn.

math.setup: Approach 1 – DCF: Firm Value = FCF / (Discount Rate - Growth Rate). Approach 2 – Multiples: Firm Value = EBIT x Average Multiple.

questions.prompt: How much do they need in synergies for the ROI to make sense?
questions.guidance: Candidate must translate the 30% ROI target over 3 years into a dollar amount. Total required profit = $4 Bn x 30% = $1.2 Bn over 3 years. Apollo's standalone net income = $250 Mn/year, so standalone 3-year profit = $750 Mn. Synergies needed = $1.2 Bn - $750 Mn = $450 Mn over 3 years.

math.setup: Required total profit = Acquisition price x ROI target. Standalone profit over 3 years = Net Income x 3. Synergy gap = Required profit - Standalone profit.
steps: Standalone profit over 3 years = $250 Mn x 3 = $750 Mn
math.answer: $450 Mn in synergies needed over 3 years

questions.prompt: How many procedures do they need to convert to Apollo for the deal to make sense?
questions.guidance: Use Exhibit 4. Under the proposed contract, every Athelas-insured patient who stays at Apollo costs Athelas $9.0K (patient pays $9.0K, Athelas pays $1.0K to Apollo = total $10.0K to Apollo). Under current contract the insurer pays $8.5K. So current Apollo patients now cost $0.5K more each. Apollo has 150K Athelas-insured procedures; extra cost = 150K x $0.5K = $75 Mn/year x 3 = $225 Mn total loss. For converted patients (currently at non-Apollo facilities paying $7.0K average): under proposed contract Athelas pays $9.0K total ($9.0K patient + $1.0K to hospital = $10.0K to Apollo) vs. previously $7.0K at non-Apollo. Net cost to Athelas increases by $2.0K per converted patient, but Apollo gains $8.0K revenue at $2.0K marginal cost, netting $6.0K gain to the combined entity per converted procedure. Total synergy needed INCLUDING loss offset: ($450 Mn needed + $225 Mn losses) / $6.0K per converted patient = $675 Mn / $6.0K = 112,500 procedures over 3 years.

math.setup: Loss on existing Apollo patients per procedure under proposed contract vs. current contract. Net gain per converted procedure to combined entity. Total conversions needed = (Synergy target + total losses on existing patients) / net gain per converted procedure.
steps: Current contract: Athelas pays Apollo $8.5K per procedure for its 150K patients
Proposed contract: Athelas pays Apollo $9.0K per procedure (patient contributes more)
Total loss on existing patients over 3 years = 150K x $0.5K x 3 = $225 Mn
Converted patients: Apollo revenue per procedure = $10.0K, marginal cost = $2.0K, Apollo net gain = $8.0K
Athelas previously paid $7.0K at non-Apollo; now pays $9.0K to Apollo, net insurer cost increase = $2.0K
Combined entity net gain per converted procedure = $8.0K - $2.0K = $6.0K
Total needed = $450 Mn (synergy target) + $225 Mn (losses) = $675 Mn
Conversions needed = $675 Mn / $6.0K per procedure = 112,500 procedures over 3 years
math.answer: 112,500 procedures converted to Apollo over 3 years

brainstorming.prompt: How can Athelas make up the additional $450 Mn in synergies needed to meet the ROI target over 3 years?

categories.name: Reduce hospital costs
ideas: Leverage Athelas' scale to negotiate better supply and pharmaceutical prices
Implement shared back-office and administrative functions
However: an insurance company is unlikely to be best positioned to reduce clinical delivery costs; medical staff resistance likely

categories.name: Reduce insurer costs
ideas: Renegotiate contract so Athelas pays Apollo less per procedure
Risk: equally reduces hospital revenues, damaging Apollo financially
Unlikely to attract new enrollees since patients see no direct benefit

categories.name: Increase combined revenues
ideas: Offer preferential pricing at Apollo to Athelas-insured patients to incentivize conversion of procedures from non-Apollo facilities
Attract new insurance lives by marketing better/lower-cost access to Apollo's high-quality care
Cross-sell: bundle insurance and hospital services
Upsell premium insurance tiers tied to Apollo access

recommendation: Bid $4.0 Bn for Apollo Hospital, supported by both DCF ($4 Bn at $400 Mn FCF / 10% discount) and comparable multiples ($750 Mn EBIT x 5.33x)

Post-acquisition, renegotiate the Athelas-Apollo contract to the proposed pricing scheme to convert non-Apollo procedures to Apollo, targeting 112,500 procedure conversions over 3 years to achieve the $450 Mn synergy target and meet the 30% 3-year ROI
risks: Need to increase Apollo's procedures by approximately 20% over 3 years; may meet resistance from medical staff on workload and culture
Nature of newly converted patients may not match Apollo's specializations or existing capacity mix
Proposed contract raises cost per existing Apollo procedure by $0.5K, creating a $225 Mn headwind that must be offset by conversion gains
Apollo's reputation for quality could be diluted if capacity is stressed by rapid volume increases
Regulatory scrutiny: vertical integration of insurer and hospital may attract antitrust or state insurance commission review
next_steps: Investigate which procedure types are most likely to convert (e.g., elective surgeries, specialist referrals)
Analyze whether the improved Apollo contract terms will attract new insurance enrollees and quantify the revenue uplift
Conduct clinical and operational due diligence on Apollo's capacity mix and staffing to validate the 200K excess-patient ceiling
Develop a physician engagement and change-management plan before announcing the new volume targets
